Agents are becoming the front door to every website.

AXE is an open, HTTP-native protocol and TypeScript SDK that lets your site declare what it can do, how to present results, what it needs to finish, and when a human must step in. You wrap functions you already have.

Agentic eXperience Engineering — because your site should smell good to agents too.

Get startedRead the spec
npm i @axe/core

The problem

Today the agent gives up and hands the task back.

The same request, twice: once against a website as it is, once against a website that declares what it can do.

Without AXE

Apply for the one-bedroom at The Meridian in Bellevue and pay the holding deposit from my checking account.

Agent opens a headless browser and starts the six-page application.

I found the unit and filled in the first pages, but the deposit form wants bank details typed into a widget I can't safely use, and I can't tell whether submitting charges you. I couldn't complete this. Please finish it yourself.

With AXE

Apply for the one-bedroom at The Meridian in Bellevue and pay the holding deposit from my checking account.

Agent calls applications.submit; the site answers needs_input accepting payment.ach-debit.

Oakridge needs a $500 refundable deposit by bank transfer. Use your checking account ending 4471?

Yes.

Agent continues with the authorization from its wallet; the site answers ok.

Done. Application APP-8812 is submitted and the deposit is received.

Where the browser gives up

Agents already try to act on websites for people. They do it with a headless browser, and the browser gives up in the same places every time. Four stories, one from each of the organizations these docs use.

A yoga studio. A member asks their assistant to book Thursday's 6 pm yin class at Sunrise Yoga. The agent loads the schedule, finds the class, and clicks "Book". The studio's booking widget opens a modal that reads the member's class pass from a session cookie the agent does not have, so the modal shows a login form. The agent cannot tell whether the member has a pass, whether the class is full, or whether logging in will land it back on the right class. It tells the member: "I found the class, but you'll need to book it yourself."

A university. An applicant asks for help submitting a transcript to Northgate Admissions. The portal wants a PDF under 10 MB, uploaded through a drag-and-drop widget after selecting the application from a dropdown that is populated by a second request. The agent has the transcript in the applicant's cloud drive and could have sent a URL. Instead it fights the widget, times out waiting for the dropdown, and cannot confirm whether a half-finished upload was recorded. It reports: "The upload page didn't respond. Please try it in your browser."

A property manager. A renter asks their agent to apply for a one-bedroom at Oakridge Rentals. The search works. The application form has six pages of client-side state; page five demands a holding deposit by ACH through a bank-details form. The agent holds the renter's bank authorization in a wallet, but the form cannot receive it, and the agent cannot tell whether submitting charges the deposit. It stops: "This needs a deposit. I can't safely enter payment details here."

An online shop. A shopper asks to return a jacket from last week's order. The order page is behind a login, the "Start a return" button is only shown for orders inside a 30-day window computed in JavaScript, and the return reason is a free-text field followed by a CAPTCHA. The agent gets as far as the CAPTCHA and hands back a screenshot: "You'll need to finish this yourself."

In every case the business logic could have done the work. The site simply had no way to say to an agent: here is what I can do, here is what I need from you to do it, and here is the one step your human has to take.

Read the full section in the docs.

How it works

The ladder: complete, ask the agent, then the human.

When an action cannot finish, the site says exactly what would unblock it, in a form the agent may already hold. Only when nothing matches does it hand off to the human, with a URL, a reason, and a token to resume. Every envelope below is real: the build runs the docs' apartment example and records what came back.

  1. 1
    ok

    The work is done. output is present.

  2. 2
    needs_input

    The site lists accepts: kinds the agent may hold, each with a schema.

  3. 3
    needs_human

    A handoff: url, instructions, what to tell the user, and a resumeToken.

The read side

Search, present, select.

Most agent journeys start with a read. The site declares which fields matter for comparison and what can be done with each result; the agent renders. The search results shown here are the output of the reference renderer in @axe/client/present, produced at build time from the docs' Bellevue example. Choose a unit and the ladder above binds that unit's id.

Rendered by toHTML. Buttons dispatch an axe:select event with the affordance's bound input; this page listens and hands it to the ladder. The second unit shows dynamic affordances: the site knows an application is already open, so it offers only a tour.

Presenting results covers pointers, attributes, pagination, freshness, and the renderers.

What you declare

Six things a site gives an agent.

Manifest

One JSON document at a fixed path: who you are, what you can do, how to authenticate, what the rules are.

Actions

Typed operations with schemas, a description written for a model, and truthful risk, readOnly, idempotent, and reversible metadata.

Display

Which fields matter when a user compares results, where the human page is, and the disclaimer that must accompany any rendering.

Affordances

What can be done with each result, with inputs pre-bound. The user's pick becomes the next call with no guesswork.

Requirements and kinds

Ask the agent first: a shared vocabulary of payloads a wallet or credential store can supply.

Handoff

The human, last: a URL that lands on the step, plain instructions, and a token to resume.

If you did search optimization in 2008, the shape is familiar. The mapping, from the docs:

SEOAXE
sitemap.xmlThe manifest at /.well-known/axe.json: everything the site can do, in one document.
Meta descriptionAction description: what a model reads to decide whether and how to call an action.
schema.org vocabularyWell-known kinds (payment.ach-debit, document.url, consent.terms): shared payload types an agent wallet can fulfill.
Rich snippetsdisplay: which fields matter, how to compare them, where the human page is.
Lighthouse and PageSpeedaxe audit: a score, a fix list, and the reasons.
Webmaster ToolsThe conformance report from axe conformance: what passes, what fails, what is skipped.
robots.txtThe AXE-Manifest and AXE-Index directives in robots.txt (discovery hints), and policies.agents (opt-in and opt-out per vendor).

Get to a passing score

There is a number to move.

Code

Wrap what you already have.

A yoga studio exposes one read-only search and one booking. These are the docs' own examples; they typecheck in the repository.

axe.ts
axe.register(
  action("classes.search", {
    title: "Search upcoming classes",
    description:
      "Find upcoming classes by date range and style. Returns up to 50 classes with start time, instructor, and spots left. Does not book anything.",
    readOnly: true,
    risk: "none",
    input: z.object({
      from: z.string().date().describe("Earliest class date, YYYY-MM-DD"),
      to: z.string().date().optional().describe("Latest class date, YYYY-MM-DD"),
      style: z.enum(["vinyasa", "yin", "hatha"]).optional().describe("Yoga style"),
    }),
    output: z.object({ classes: z.array(ClassSchema) }),
    display: {
      kind: "list",
      items: "/classes",
      item: {
        id: "/id",
        title: "/title",
        subtitle: "/instructor",
        url: "/url",
        attributes: [
          { label: "Starts", path: "/startsAt", format: "datetime", compare: "lower-better" },
          { label: "Style", path: "/style", format: "text" },
          { label: "Spots left", path: "/spotsLeft", format: "number", compare: "higher-better" },
        ],
      },
      suggestedComparison: ["Starts", "Spots left"],
      disclaimer:
        "Availability changes quickly. Confirm on the class page before planning around it.",
    },
    examples: [{ input: { from: "2026-10-01" }, output: { classes: CLASSES } }],
    handler: async ({ input }) => ({
      classes: CLASSES.filter(
        (c) =>
          c.startsAt.slice(0, 10) >= input.from &&
          (!input.to || c.startsAt.slice(0, 10) <= input.to) &&
          (!input.style || c.style === input.style),
      ),
    }),
  }),
);
descriptions.ts
axe.register(
  action("classes.book", {
    title: "Book a class",
    description: good,
    risk: "medium",
    idempotent: true,
    reversible: true,
    auth: "user",
    input: z
      .object({
        classId: z.string().describe("Class id from classes.search, e.g. 'c_101'"),
        spot: z
          .enum(["mat", "reformer"])
          .optional()
          .describe("Equipment preference; defaults to 'mat'"),
      })
      .strict(),
    output: z.object({
      bookingId: z.string(),
      startsAt: z.string().datetime().describe("Confirmed class start, ISO 8601"),
      creditsRemaining: z
        .number()
        .int()
        .describe("Credits left on the member's pass after this booking"),
    }),
    examples: [
      {
        input: { classId: "c_101" },
        output: { bookingId: "b_5531", startsAt: "2026-10-01T14:00:00Z", creditsRemaining: 7 },
      },
    ],
    handler: async ({ input, context }) =>
      bookings.reserve(input.classId, context.onBehalfOf!, input.spot),
  }),
);

Mount it

server-express.ts
import express from "express";
import { axeExpress } from "@axe/express";
import { axe } from "./axe";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

// Serves /.well-known/axe.json and every /axe/* endpoint. Everything else falls through.
app.use(axeExpress(axe));

app.get("/", (_req, res) => {
  res.send("Sunrise Yoga Studio");
});

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
app.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`Listening on http://localhost:${port}`);
});
route.ts
import { axeNext } from "@axe/next";
import { axe } from "./axe";

export const { GET, POST, OPTIONS } = axeNext(axe);
server-fetch.ts
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { serve } from "@hono/node-server";
import { axeFetch } from "@axe/fetch";
import { axe } from "./axe";

const app = new Hono();
const handler = axeFetch(axe);

app.all("/axe/*", (c) => handler(c.req.raw));
app.get("/.well-known/axe.json", (c) => handler(c.req.raw));
app.get("/", (c) => c.text("Sunrise Yoga Studio"));

serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000) });

Then three commands

npx axe init

Writes an axe.ts with one read-only action and the mount file for your framework.

npx axe conformance http://localhost:3000

Runs the protocol suite against your server and prints a pass/fail table. This is how you know you are done.

npx axe mcp http://localhost:3000

Serves your site to Claude Desktop or Claude Code as an MCP server, one tool per action.
